newsitem.title: UK: BT insists no significance to NTT talks.
newsitem.headline: BT insists no significance to NTT talks.

text.p: British Telecommunications (BT) insisted on Friday that talks between its chairman and executives from Japanese telecoms giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp were of no particular significance.

Since the talks were announced on Thursday, speculation has swept the market that BT, which along with its American partner MCI Communications has been openly courting NTT, may be on the brink of a link-up with the telecoms titan.
But a BT spokesman told Reuters: "That meeting was of no particular significance. We have regular contacts at that level and will continue to do so with NTT and others."
But some analysts speculated that BT, keen to get a foothold in the lucrative Asian telecoms markets, may hammer out a deal with NTT quite soon.
"I think that they are quite close to it," said John Tysoe, telecoms analyst at brokers SocGen Strauss Turnbull. But he added: "That is just instict."
One analyst even said he had made a bet with a colleague that a deal would be signed or announced before the end of February. But others were split.
"It's one of those issues that it would be nice to put to bed," said Chris McFadden, telecoms analyst at Merrill Lynch.
"You would expect in the next 12-18 months something to happen," he said, but added: "If it happened tomorrow, we'd be all presently surprised."

Dismissing as a mere "courtship ritual" NTT's statement that it might prefer to branch out into the global international market on its own, analysts do agree on one thing -- NTT will want to be calling the shots on this deal.

BT's proposed $20 billion merger with MCI, which the company hopes to have approved in September, may also hinder any imminent announcement of a deal with NTT. Regulatory clearance for the huge deal hinges on whether the British telecoms market is as open as the American one. Adding a Japanese monopoly operator to the equation may cloud the issue.
"It depends what sort of tie-up we're looking at," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
"It is quite possible that they may talk about a memorandum of understanding. But in terms of any tangible, real tie-up, I would put it later in the year."
BT's chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield is also travelling to Japan at the end of this month, part of a regular trip where he is likely to meet NTT executives.
BT has had an office in Japan for 10 years and this year sent its first regional director to Tokyo in a move to highlight the growing importance of the area.
It already has a minor link with one of NTT's units, NTT Data, which distributes its Concert Internet Plus services.
